readings.title: A rehearsal room for more than one group
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A community music centre had one soundproof room and several groups who wanted it. The first booking calendar favoured people able to call during office hours. The central difficulty was limited access to popular evening slots. Workers with daytime jobs often learned about free times after another group had booked them. The organizers knew that a tidy plan in an office might not match what happened in an ordinary week.

The group first tried an online and paper booking trial. The centre released slots at a known time and accepted requests at the desk or through a simple online form. They therefore listened to people who used the place at different times, including those who seldom attended formal meetings.

The trial showed clear release times improved fairness. Different groups could plan ahead, although some still needed a regular hour to prepare for public performances. In response, the group adopted rotating priority for repeated bookings. Staff kept a small number of continuing sessions but rotated the most requested evening times among groups. The notes did not remove every disagreement, but they made the reasons for the next decision easier to explain.

The broader lesson was clear: shared spaces need transparent rules. The centre could not offer every group its preferred hour, but it could explain how decisions were made and revised. Keeping a record of small changes also helped the team distinguish a temporary setback from a lasting problem. For the people involved in a rehearsal room for more than one group, the result was useful because it connected an everyday difficulty with a change they could see and discuss. No one claimed that a single trial could settle every question. The group planned to watch what happened over time and to explain any further changes openly.

readings.title: A mural planned with local residents
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
An artist was invited to paint a wall beside a busy square. The first sketch used colours residents liked but ignored how the wall was used. The central difficulty was a design covering a useful notice area. Community groups posted event information there, and removing that space would make ordinary announcements harder to find. A first impression was not enough to tell the whole story, because different people approached the service in different ways.

The group first tried walk-throughs and short drawing sessions. The artist asked residents what they wanted to keep, invited ideas from children and measured the part needed for public notices. The team compared comments with direct observations rather than assuming that the loudest opinion represented everyone.

The trial showed the notice area mattered to many groups. The artist learned that a practical surface could be part of the square’s identity rather than an obstacle to art. In response, the group adopted a mural framing a new noticeboard. The final design left clear space for announcements and used painted patterns to draw attention to them. Some suggestions were inexpensive, while others would have required a change to staffing or equipment.

The broader lesson was clear: public art can respect existing public uses. The project improved the wall without making a familiar community function disappear. The final proposal remained open to revision when new information became available. For the people involved in a mural planned with local residents, the result was useful because it connected an everyday difficulty with a change they could see and discuss. No one claimed that a single trial could settle every question. The group planned to watch what happened over time and to explain any further changes openly. This careful pace mattered: people were more willing to support a decision when they understood which observations had shaped it and which concerns remained.

readings.title: Captions at a small theatre
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A local theatre wanted more people to enjoy its performances. It considered captions but assumed they would distract the audience. The central difficulty was uncertainty about where captions should appear. A screen beside the stage helped some viewers but forced others to turn away from the actors. Several participants valued the original aim even though they questioned the first method chosen to reach it.

The group first tried a caption trial from several seats. Audience members with different hearing needs watched a short rehearsal and described what they could read comfortably. Short conversations after the activity revealed details that a written form had failed to capture.

The trial showed seat position changed the viewing experience. The same caption placement worked from the middle rows but not from seats close to the side wall. In response, the group adopted clear seat guidance and adjusted display. The theatre moved the screen slightly and identified seats from which both captions and performers were easy to see. The people responsible made their limits clear and invited others to describe any unintended effects.

The broader lesson was clear: access changes need real audience feedback. The team learned more from a rehearsal with viewers than from guessing what a screen might look like in an empty hall. This approach gave the group a practical basis for its next round of work. For the people involved in captions at a small theatre, the result was useful because it connected an everyday difficulty with a change they could see and discuss. No one claimed that a single trial could settle every question. The group planned to watch what happened over time and to explain any further changes openly. This careful pace mattered: people were more willing to support a decision when they understood which observations had shaped it and which concerns remained.

readings.title: A craft market tells makers stories
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A weekend craft market displayed handmade objects with prices but little other information. Visitors admired the work yet rarely spoke with makers. The central difficulty was labels that omitted how objects were made. Many buyers could not tell which materials were local or why a simple-looking item took several hours to finish. The project began on a small scale so that its organizers could learn before making a permanent commitment.

The group first tried short maker notes beside selected stalls. Sellers wrote two sentences about a technique or material and invited questions without requiring every visitor to start a conversation. They noted both benefits and costs, including the time that volunteers or staff needed to give.

The trial showed visitors asked more specific questions. The notes helped people notice details, although makers still wanted enough time to sell rather than explain continuously. In response, the group adopted optional demonstrations at set times. The market added brief demonstrations so interested visitors could learn more without interrupting each purchase. The public summary described what had changed and what questions had not yet been answered.

The broader lesson was clear: context can deepen appreciation without pressure. A short explanation connected objects to human work while leaving room for visitors to explore at their own pace. Readers could therefore judge the decision by its evidence rather than by a promise of perfect results. For the people involved in a craft market tells makers stories, the result was useful because it connected an everyday difficulty with a change they could see and discuss. No one claimed that a single trial could settle every question. The group planned to watch what happened over time and to explain any further changes openly. This careful pace mattered: people were more willing to support a decision when they understood which observations had shaped it and which concerns remained.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
Public art can change how people notice a familiar place. When an artist planned a mural beside a town square, the first sketch covered a wall used for community notices. Residents liked the colours but wanted to keep a place for announcements. The artist held short drawing sessions and asked different groups what the wall meant to them. The final design framed a new noticeboard instead of replacing it. Visitors could enjoy the painting and still find information about local events. The project showed that listening to practical concerns does not limit creativity. It can help an artwork become part of the life around it.
translation.explanation: 注意instead of和does not limit的准确表达。
translation.referenceAnswer: 公共艺术能够改变人们看待熟悉地点的方式。一位艺术家计划在城镇广场旁绘制壁画时，初稿覆盖了一面用于张贴社区通知的墙。居民喜欢其中的色彩，却希望保留公告位置。艺术家组织了简短的绘画讨论，询问不同群体这面墙对他们意味着什么。最终设计把新公告栏作为画面的一部分，而没有取代它。访客既能欣赏画作，也能找到当地活动信息。项目表明，倾听实际顾虑不会限制创造力，反而能使艺术作品融入周围生活。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to an arts committee proposing a mural for a community square. Explain how residents could contribute ideas and how the wall could still display local notices.
writing.explanation: 范文覆盖居民参与和公告栏保留。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Arts Committee,
I welcome the plan for a mural beside the square. Before a final design is chosen, the artist could hold two short drawing sessions at different times. Children, shopkeepers and older residents might notice different features of the place. People who cannot attend should be able to leave a written idea at the library. The artist can then explain which suggestions have shaped the design.
The wall currently carries useful notices, so I suggest building a clear noticeboard into the mural rather than removing it. Painted lines could guide visitors toward information about local events. We should measure the space needed for readable notices before work begins. After the mural is finished, the committee could ask whether both the artwork and the announcements are easy to enjoy and use.
Yours sincerely,
A neighbour
